A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same EAPrivacy benchmark. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and matchable across renumbering and relocation, supporting a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 16 LLM configurations across four privacy tiers, including numerical results, variability estimates, and qualitative failure analyses.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds PDDL-versus-text experiments, an in-context learning comparison, and analyses stratified by human agreement.

M1.justification: v3 Appendix D introduces a simple inference-time ICL solution that augments queries with three examples: one nonsensitive case and two sensitive cases. This procedure is absent from v1; the underlying four-tier benchmark and action definitions remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v3 Appendix C adds a simplified text-only Tier 1 scenario in which the target container's objects are explicitly listed, removing the spatial localization requirement of the corresponding PDDL task. The original physical domains, four tiers, and existing privacy-benchmark coverage are retained.

E2.justification: The original 16 LLM configurations remain. v3 Table 5 adds ICL-versus-unaugmented comparisons for six Gemini/GPT-5 configurations, while Appendix E adds a quantified human-rater performance baseline for Tier 2, reporting overall MAD of 0.61.

E3.justification: Supplementary protocols now compare PDDL and explicit item-list inputs at 10- and 30-item configurations, test three-shot prompting at 30 items, and evaluate results within human-agreement strata. The original evaluation settings remain; these are additional controlled evaluations rather than documented changes to the original runs.

E4.justification: v3 substantially expands benchmark validation: Appendix C tests the effect of requiring spatially structured input, Appendix D tests whether few-shot examples mitigate identification failures, and Appendix E examines dependence on annotator agreement. The original clutter analyses, thinking comparisons, and failure case studies are retained.

E5.justification: v3 newly quantifies annotation agreement: Tier 4 has 68% unanimous and 32% four-of-five agreement, while 108 Tier 2 ratings are grouped by across-rater variance. The original model-standard-deviation table is unchanged, and no increase in repeated runs or seeds is documented.

E6.justification: Original headline results and the full results table are retained, but Tables 3–10 add substantial numerical evidence. Examples include average Tier 1 MOR of 0.40 for PDDL versus 0.78 for text at 10 items, and Gemini Flash MOR of 0.1782 without ICL versus 0.3363 with ICL at 30 items. New agreement-stratified results are also reported; some new aggregate values conflict with retained tables.

T1.justification: The MOR definition and formal ONC definition are unchanged, with the latter moving from Appendix J to Appendix L. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs, and the new empirical analyses introduce no substantive mathematical development.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the four-tier benchmark contribution and central claims about deficient physical-world privacy reasoning, asymmetric conservatism, and adverse thinking effects. The added experiments support or qualify these claims without redefining the paper's main contribution.

C2.justification: Section 4.5 softens serious ethical-failure language to potential risks relative to majority human judgments. Appendix E explains that models align closely on unanimous Tier 4 items and suggests caution when humans disagree. Appendices C–D add interpretations concerning spatial reasoning and model-dependent ICL benefits and tradeoffs.

D1.justification: v3 supplies a text-control prompt, specifies the three-example ICL composition, and adds annotation collection details, including Google Forms and campus recruitment. Its abstract reports dataset availability at Graph-COM/EAPrivacy, whereas v1 promises future release at frinkleko/EAPrivacy. Actual repository contents cannot be verified from the PDFs.

R1.justification: v3 adds Shao et al.'s PrivacyLens citation and explicitly distinguishes its communication-oriented actions, such as sending emails, from physically grounded actions. The remaining references and broader research positioning are retained; PrivacyLens is not newly evaluated as a baseline.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section sequence are largely preserved. Changes include a motivation sentence, localized revisions to Tier 4 interpretation, two new appendix sections, expansion of the annotation appendix, updated cross-references, and the conference-publication header.

P2.justification: v3 substantially expands the visual presentation with PDDL/text comparison tables, an ICL comparison table, agreement distributions and stratified performance tables, a variance histogram, and a text-prompt box. Existing plots and tables are retained and reflowed; the new displays provide additional analytical views rather than merely renumbering existing material.

improvement.justification: The controlled input comparison, practical ICL baseline, and quantified annotation agreement improve validation and transparency beyond v1. These gains are limited by new reporting inconsistencies: Table 8 labels values matching retained Tier 4 accuracies as lower-is-better MAD, and Table 9 reports Gemini Flash Tier 2 MAD as 1.28 versus 1.32 in retained Table 1 without explanation. The additions provide a modest net benefit, but do not establish a substantial overall improvement.
